À Saint-Michel, des résidents cherchent: In Saint-Michel, residents are seeking to be heard and to give local political participation new meaning.
Des résident·es de Saint-Michel se réuni: Saint-Michel residents gather at the Carrefour populaire to discuss municipal politics and voter turnout. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
À Saint-Michel, j’ai voulu comprendre po: In Saint-Michel, I wanted to understand why voter turnout remains so low despite years of community efforts. In the last municipal election, fewer than one in four voters showed up.
J’ai passé la soirée du 24 octobre au Ca: I spent the evening of October 24 at the Carrefour populaire de Saint-Michel, where residents, candidates and community workers came together over a meal to talk about engagement and local politics. There I met young people, residents and people working on the ground who, each in their own way, are trying to give their neighbourhood its voice back.
Ce reportage s’appuie sur leurs paroles,: This report draws on their words, their observations and their hopes.
<strong>Vendredi 24 octobre. La suite 10: Friday, October 24. Suite 100 at the Carrefour populaire de Saint-Michel is overflowing. The tables are set, the chairs packed tight, the murmurs impatient, and the soup is still warming in the kitchen. It is 5:15 p.m. The young organizers from the neighbourhood roundtable, Vivre Saint-Michel en santé (VSMS), confer in low voices, going over the evening’s schedule one more time.
Une demi-heure plus tard, quand <l1>Aya: Half an hour later, when <l1>Aya Boucenna</l1>, a La Converse journalist and member of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, and Wismy Noster of VSMS take the microphone to open the gathering, the room is packed to the brim. Before them sit Saint-Michel residents from all walks of life, here to talk about municipal politics – a subject that often struggles to draw people in here.
En effet, dans ce quartier de l’est mont: Indeed, in this east-end Montréal neighbourhood, where <l1>according to Elections Canada, fewer than one in four voters turned out for the 2021 municipal election</l1>, a gathering like this is far from ordinary.
Fragmenté et enclavé par l’autoroute 40: Fragmented and hemmed in by Highway 40 and the Francon and Miron quarries, Saint-Michel is one of the most densely populated and most multicultural areas of Montréal.
Le portrait réalisé en 2024 par VSMS dan: The 2024 profile produced by VSMS as part of the neighbourhood’s 2025-2029 strategic plan indicates that nearly 70% of residents are from immigrant backgrounds and that more than 60 languages are spoken here. It is also one of the youngest boroughs – one resident in three is under 25 – and one of the most precarious: the median income is 30% below the Montréal average.
Le quartier a longtemps été un point d’a: The neighbourhood has long been a point of arrival for newcomers to Montréal: Haitians, North Africans, Filipinos, Tamils and Bangladeshis. But for many, Saint-Michel is only a stopover. According to Christian Toussaint, a coordination officer at VSMS, “it’s a transit neighbourhood where people arrive, settle for a few years, then leave as soon as they can afford to.” This constant movement, he adds, “makes mobilizing difficult,” forcing the team to “start the outreach work over and over again – it’s a perpetual fight.”
Cette soirée est la dernière d’une série: This evening is the last in a series of four events meant to revive civic participation. It is an ambitious bet for a neighbourhood whose turnout rate is among the lowest in Montréal. In 2021, only 24.3% of registered voters in Saint-Michel cast a ballot.
Mohamed Mimoun, directeur du Forum Jeune: Mohamed Mimoun, director of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, points out that “in a borough with a high rate of immigration, there isn’t that culture of voting.” Asked on the sidelines of the evening, Mr. Mimoun says “there are people who aren’t even aware that there are municipal elections” and that “we don’t prepare [them] to exercise their right to vote.” For him, “people don’t see how their vote will make a difference. And sometimes they don’t see the difference between the candidates.”

Along the same lines, Christian Toussaint, a coordination officer at VSMS in charge of the culture, sports and leisure file, speaks of a problem of democratic transmission: “Many come from countries where they had no right to vote. Some are afraid of it, others don’t understand the system. That’s why we have to do education all the time.”
Mais le contexte migratoire ne suffit pa: But the migration context alone doesn’t explain the low turnout in municipal elections. To go beyond that observation, VSMS has organized a series of activities in recent weeks – election cafés, information sessions, public debates – to try to mend the bond between residents and institutions.
Ce souper-discussion devait convaincre l: This dinner-discussion was meant to convince Saint-Michel residents that municipal politics belongs to them too. In the end, it mainly gave participants a space to explain why so many of them have turned away from it.
Une scène improvisée, dans un coin de la: A makeshift stage in a corner of the room was set aside for the four candidates vying for the Saint-Michel electoral district on the Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension borough council.
Les quatre candidat·es en lice dans le d: The four candidates running in the Saint-Michel electoral district talk with residents. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche.
Éric Allen Jr. (Action Montréal), Sylvai: Éric Allen Jr. (Action Montréal), Sylvain Gariépy (Ensemble Montréal), Jean-François Lalonde (Projet Montréal) and Nounthia Renord (Futur Montréal) came to talk with residents. The topics put up for debate were access to housing, local economic development, social development, mobility, safety, youth, and the opening up of the isolated sector.
Le micro circule dans l’auditoire. « Bon: The microphone makes its way through the audience. “Hello, my name is Samir Souanes, I’m 21. I’d like to ask a question about homelessness. I’ve noticed that lately the rate has gone up,” says a young man. The panellists pass the microphone along, each explaining their party’s vision – calling for more social housing, as Mr. Lalonde does; or more resources for the organizations tasked with fighting homelessness, say Mr. Gariépy and M<sup>s</sup>. Renord; or even the creation of a dedicated program for these populations, in Mr. Allen’s view.
Sans interrompre les échanges, un repas: Without interrupting the discussion, a hot meal is served: fragrant rice, grilled chicken and salad. “A real feast,” sighs one resident.
Dans la salle, la moyenne d’âge dépasse: In the room, the average age is over 40. Apart from a few members of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, young people are missing. Their absence does not go unnoticed. Several speakers stress the need to find new ways to get them interested in these issues.
<strong>« C’est quoi l’utilité de voter: “What’s the point of voting if they’re not going to listen to us?”
Parmi les rares jeunes présents, Mark Da:
Among the few young people present, Mark Dagala, 25, shares how he feels.
“Yes, I’m going to vote, despite the results maybe being a little… maybe biased,” he says. He searches for his words: “Even though we talk about our needs, in a way they get ignored.”
Ses amis, ajoute-t-il, ne votent pas. «: His friends, he adds, don’t vote. “They say, ‘What’s the point of voting if they’re not really going to listen to us?’” He points to the lack of consultation in some local decisions, notably the bike lane project rolled out in the summer of 2022: “When we saw the bike lane on First Avenue, nobody had consulted us. People felt abandoned.”
L’enjeu de la consultation a d’ailleurs: The issue of consultation was on the meeting’s agenda, and candidates spoke of the failings of the city council’s citizen consultation process. In their remarks, Sylvain Gariépy and Éric Allen Jr. also cited the First Avenue bike lane project.
Et ce n’est pas le seul déficit, relève: And that’s not the only shortfall, says Mark Dagala. “I think there’s been a complete abandonment. Funding was moved to neighbourhoods that bring a bigger return, like Villeray or the Plateau. We were an afterthought,” he believes.
Un autre jeune Michelois, Ahmed El Moudd: Another young resident of Saint-Michel, Ahmed El Moudden, a former École Converse journalist who has been involved with the Forum Jeunesse for a decade, echoes his fellow resident’s words. “Ten years ago, young people were very engaged. They got together, talked about political issues. Today, they believe less in Saint-Michel and in politics in general,” he says before the room, which listens closely.
Autour des tables, plusieurs acquiescent: Around the tables, several people nod. Ahmed explains this disengagement by broken promises: “There are a lot of causes young people pushed over the last 10 years that didn’t really go anywhere.” He cites the Francon quarry, that vast stone pit at the heart of the neighbourhood, still an empty wasteland: “We were hugely involved in that. There was very little progress. The City abandoned young people,” he laments.
Le cas de la carrière Francon, dont la t: The case of the Francon quarry, whose size equals 98 soccer fields, comes up in several speeches. Since quarrying ended in 1986, the site, which the City has owned since 1981, has been used as a municipal warehouse and, above all, as a snow dump. Saint-Michel residents are calling for the site to be redeveloped, and a public consultation was even held by the Office de consultation publique de Montréal (OCPM) in 2008, followed by a citizen participation process launched in 2016. In 2018, VSMS developed the citizen-led project <l1>Francon, cœur de notre quartier</l1>, but no political decision has come to make the local population’s dream a reality.
L’impression d’abandon revient dans plus: The feeling of abandonment comes up in several testimonies.
Résidente du secteur Est de Saint-Michel: A resident of the East sector of Saint-Michel, Sugir Selliah describes an area losing its services. “Not only is the Saint-Michel neighbourhood the most disadvantaged of the borough’s three neighbourhoods, but the East sector [of the district] is even more disadvantaged,” she says. M<sup>s</sup>. Selliah bemoans a “glaring lack of green space,” “undervalued young people” and “the loss of many services,” illustrated, she explains, by community organizations leaving after the CSDM took back the premises where they were housed.
Elle souligne aussi le fossé entre élus: She also points to the gap between elected officials and residents: “People in Saint-Michel feel less listened to because the needs being put forward are out of touch. Elected officials have to go to the people, go door to door, show up in person.”
Au fil des échanges, les résidents se mo: As the discussion goes on, residents show themselves to be clear-eyed about the neighbourhood’s issues and eager to be heard. Between speeches, you can hear the clink of cutlery and the quiet laughter of a few volunteers. In the room, Wismy Noster, a coordination officer at VSMS, watches the exchanges. For him, every table, every question asked is already progress. “In five years, this is the first time we’ve managed to mobilize this many people,” he confides.
Mais il reste lucide : « La mobilisation: But he remains clear-eyed: “Mobilizing is never easy, especially in a neighbourhood like Saint-Michel. Many people juggle several jobs. When you invite them to civic activities, the answer is often: ‘Sir, I have to put food on the table.’” Everyday constraints partly explain the low turnout, he says: “It’s not disinterest, it’s exhaustion.”
Vers 21 h, la salle se vide lentement. L: Around 9 p.m., the room slowly empties. The chairs are folded, the microphones unplugged. Outside, the streets of Saint-Michel go quiet. Only the cafés of Petit Maghreb stay lively, and a few workers wait for the bus on Pie-IX. In this neighbourhood where voting is never a reflex, life goes back to its routine.
